articles.title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece

Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine. The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. That exchange captured the lesson of the trip: while many governments in the region welcome U.S. assistance in countering transnational criminal organizations, few have publicly embraced Hegseth’s approach of using military forces to “kill” versus “capture” suspected traffickers. And, while Hegseth returned with new defense agreements, the details of those agreements show the limits of which governments are willing to cooperate and how far they are willing to go in the Pentagon’s renewed “war” on drugs. Hegseth began his travels into the region with an unannounced stop in Venezuela, where he signed a binational defense agreement with Venezuelan’s Minister of Defense General Gonzalez Lopez, with Venezuela’s Acting President Delcy Rodriguez watching. articles.title: Are US aircraft carriers becoming $22 billion liabilities?
articles.description: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. Armchair admirals like to quote presidents demanding to know “where are the carriers?” when trouble erupts somewhere around the world. That’s why there was a wave of stories last week when the U.S. carrier presence near Iran jumped from two to three. It was “a dramatic show of military might as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war,” the Associated Press reported November 16. Two days later, when one of the carriers left the region, not so much. What had been a “dramatic show of military might” on Monday turned into a mere “shuffling of aircraft carriers in the Middle East” by Wednesday, the AP said . Such high-seas tracking should come as no surprise. Crow’s nests and watchstanders have been replaced by satellites and websites . There are even websites dedicated to locating the U.S. Navy’s 11 aircraft carriers. These steel-hulled behemoths have been heralded as “4.5 acres of sovereign U.S. territory.” But they’re steadily becoming a 4.5-acre bull’s-eye. articles.title: Isolating the Taliban has become an unhelpful virtue signaling exercise
articles.description: Before traveling to Afghanistan last month, I heard plenty of warnings about the potential dangers of my trip. I’d been there before as a congressional staffer, but this was my first time back under the new leadership. Russia is the only country that has officially recognized the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, and the U.S. embassy in Kabul remains closed five years after American troops left the country. If I needed official security assistance, the closest U.S. connection would be hundreds of miles away. My security aside – and to be clear, I felt far safer in Afghanistan this trip than I did when U.S. troops ran the country – it’s short-sighted to ostracize and isolate the government in Kabul. It leaves the international community with no levers for influence and impact. And when there’s no relationship, there’s no incentive to change, which is why Jan Egeland, Secretary-General of the Norwegian Refugee Council, continues to urge European, North American, and other Western countries to reopen their embassies in Kabul and engage directly with government authorities in Afghanistan. Just hours after the announcement, Bradesco analysts upgraded Brazilian equities. articles.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
articles.description: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the

articles.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
articles.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
articles.description: Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”. Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
articles.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Continue reading...

Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. articles.title: Why I love Budapest in winter: ‘Gloomy days call for a plunge in one of the city’s ornate bathhouses’
articles.description: A neighbourhood that transforms into a living advent calendar, hot chocolate beneath chandeliers and 16th-century baths – Hungary’s capital is full of winter warmth Each December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
articles.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. articles.title: The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon
articles.description: Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes. It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He aske

articles.title: I spent 69 hours building Lego – here are the best sets for Christmas
articles.description: From Bluey and KPop Demon Hunters to Star Wars, Hogwarts and a working pinball machine, there’s a build to delight everyone • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 Lego may have been around for almost a hundred years, but it’s as popular as ever. Don’t take our word for it: we asked kids , teens and tweens what they wanted for Christmas this year, and Lego made it on to every single list. But with a range of collaborations with Star Wars, Harry Potter and other classic nerdy franchises, there’s plenty for (not so) grownups to get excited about as well. So when I was asked to try out some of Lego’s latest and most exciting launches, I jumped at the chance. I’ve spent the last few months turning my flat into my own personal Legoland. I built set after set until my fingers were sore and my patience thin (69hrs 31mins in total), all in the name of finding the best sets for all ages. From KPop Demon Hunters to Lando Norris’s helmet and even a retro-style pinball machine, here are the best Lego gifts for 2026. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sinister signs, suicidal shepherds and a sensational six-hour song: Ragnar Kjartansson’s art is heroically human
articles.description: Goodwood Art Foundation The Icelandic artist’s enigmatic monuments, melancholic landscape paintings and never-ending love song are witty, moving and ravishingly conceptual Live in the gallery a man in a dark suit and white shoes leans cabaret-style against a piano and sings about his one great love. “Jenny kissed me,” he intones in a voice both melodic and casually conversational. He croons the words of this love song again, and again, and again. Icelandic artist Ragnar Kjartansson’s durational performance (which means it takes a heck of a long time) is beguiling and beautiful. It’s also a brilliant interpretation of a small masterpiece of English Romantic poetry, Jenny Kiss’d Me, by Leigh Hunt : “Jenny kissed me when we met / Jumping from the chair she sat in.” The poet demands that “Time, you thief” write this down so that he can keep this memory of a perfect moment of love. Continue reading...

articles.title: I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating? | Leading questions
articles.description: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but, for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. articles.title: Dressmaker review – delightful business sim is a cut above
articles.description: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. articles.title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
articles.description: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. articles.title: Why I love Aix-en-Provence in winter: sweet treats and people watching in the quintessential Provençal city
articles.description: Market stalls are laden with local delicacies in the run-up to Christmas, while the city’s elegant cafes make the perfect spot to sit and watch the world go by Famous for its fabulous fruit and vegetable markets, Aix-en-Provence extends its stalls in winter to include les treize desserts de Noël , the 13 desserts of a traditional Provençal Christmas. I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. Also displayed alongside the usual Nativity figures in the churches and tourist office, these feature hundreds of Provençal characters including bakers, wet nurses, beekeepers, a pétanque player and the artist Paul Céz

articles.title: Slow internet? The best wifi extenders and mesh systems to boost your home network – tested
articles.description: We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home • The best office chairs Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. Continue reading...

articles.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
articles.description: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
articles.description: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johns

articles.title: Banish gloom with Paul Foot’s teetering towers of nonsense in fizzy show The Future

The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless. Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. articles.title: Country diary: Introducing Siccar Point, a true rock star of the geology world | Amy-Jane Beer
articles.description: Berwickshire: Between the grey and the red formations, a staggering 65 million years passed. And the Scottish man who figured this out put science into a spin “Who wants to see some reeeally important rocks?” The question sorts my holiday companions into two distinct types, and the self-selecting nerds set out on a blustery clifftop walk. To the north-east, the 320m-year-old volcanic doorstop of Bass Rock contrasts with the edgy artifice of Torness nuclear power station, gleaming in low sun like a radioactive Lego brick. We’re going in search of an even more consequential contrast, but one that is a little harder to see. A series of interpretation stations on the path to Siccar Point encourages us to notice two distinct rock types, old red sandstone and greywacke , and to understand that each was formed in different ways at different times. The greywacke originated in a Silurian ocean 435m years ago, the sandstone in hot deserts of the late Devonian period, 370m years ago. It’s also important to understand that, given enough time, rock can be lifted, rotated, folded and weathered away. That’s what happened to the greywacke, long before the sandstone was laid down on top. Continue r

articles.description: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns. The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.” Continue reading...

The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say. And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. It is by no means a traditional episode, almost completely dismissing the tone of everything that came before it. It seems an oddly timed endeavour, the week before large swathes of the populace either drag a plastic one down from the loft or in from outside one brutally cut down in its prime. But mine is not to reason why; mine is to stand in front of the news that we are getting a new forest and say, “Oh man, that’s brilliant, that is.” Continue reading...

articles.title: They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson | Robert Hutton
articles.description: He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works? What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays. But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s form

articles.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
articles.description: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to t

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Children’s Booker prize: everyone is a winner | Editorial
articles.description: In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked “Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize , as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote. The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue re

articles.title: How to restore dignity to the world of work | Letters
articles.description: Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley , Hartley Dean and Peter Thornton John Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become ( A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November ) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if. I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. Because arguably, that’s what underpins all of this: we’ve all been cynically inveigled into a bargain that can never be fulfilled. Continue reading...

articles.title: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters
articles.description: Willemina Rietsema , a GP, says no explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Carrie Eckersley thinks we need to consider the wider context in which symptoms develop Regarding Huw Green’s article ( How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?, 22 November ), the body and the mind/brain have strong connections both ways. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around. However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. No explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Continue reading...

articles.title: Abusers are not ‘other’ – they are all around us | Letters
articles.description: Male sexual violence against women is fuelled by misogyny, writes Sarah Mulholland The courage of Joanne Young is powerful, and it could be pivotal ( Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers, 20 November ). The publicity given to high-profile cases such as those of Russell Brand, Jeffrey Epstein and Mohamed Al Fayed is understandable, but it runs the risk of serving as a convenient deflector, allowing us to comfort ourselves that rapists and sexual abusers are somehow “other”. Indeed, one of the most pernicious rape myths is the belief that rape is perpetrated by men of a different social or economic status, of a different ethnicity or culture – outsiders from whom we can distance ourselves. Continue reading...

articles.title: Try these long novels for size | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to the Saturday magazine’s list of 20 long books for short days with their suggestions Sadly, your list of 20 long books for the short winter days ( Light in the dark, 21 November ), leaves no room at the inn for the Chums of Chance, the late 19th-century airship bods aboard the Inconvenience who provide lift-off for Thomas Pynchon’s 2006 Moby-Dick of a novel, Against the Day (1,085 pages – take that, Lucy Ellmann ). From page 3, when Pugnax the dog is found reading The Princess Casamassima by Henry James, thus igniting the book’s anarchical fascination and signalling its chaotic energy, the carnival of characters crossing continents and genres as conspirators and pursuers of conspirators are vivid, vital and funny. For a condensed read, try the 89-year-old Tom’s latest, Shadow Ticket (2026, a slip of a thing at 352 pages) where law enforcement pursues a big cheese. Joe Keaney Manchester Continue reading...

articles.title: Martin Rowson on the Conservatives and Brexit – cartoon
articles.description: Continue reading...

articles.title: Renée Slegers leaves job as Arsenal Women’s coach after dismal run of results
articles.description: Club languishing sixth in WSL after six home draws Held high hopes of mounting title challenge this term Renée Slegers has left her job as Arsenal Women’s head coach after a dismal set of results, with the club saying she has gone by mutual consent. The 37-year-old had been under contract until 2029 after signing a three-and-a-half-year deal in January but six consecutive home draws in the Women’s Super League this season have left Arsenal sixth, 12 points behind the leaders, Chelsea, and eight points adrift of a European place. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fiery Hamilton-Leclerc lineup casts doubt on Ferrari functioning in a title fight
articles.description: Costly on-track clashes have caused tensions to simmer and team need recent talks to tell at Sunday’s Qatar Grand Prix There is an unmistakable air of deja vu heading into the Qatar Grand Prix and with it an intense scrutiny that might be considered unusual for a dead-rubber weekend. Yet for Ferrari, who are the subject of the attention after costly on-track incidents between the teammates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, more pertinent is how it might play out if the conflicts are not resolved and the Scuderia are in a title fight next season. Hamilton and Leclerc clashed on track at the last round in Las Vegas, only two weeks after similarly contesting a place in Mexico cost them a potential one-two. The team principal Fred Vasseur was furious then, saying it displayed a lack of respect for the team and was unacceptable. They held talks to resolve the issue at the next round in Brazil. Continue reading...

articles.title: Harry Redknapp’s big-race hope Taurus Bay follows in hoofprints of Jukebox Man
articles.description: Newbury winner is victorious for former football manager in same race as last year’s King George VI Chase hero Harry Redknapp’s prospects of seeing a Grade One winner in his colours this season improved substantially at Newbury on Friday as Taurus Bay, making only his second start over fences, gave weight and a half-length beating to Royal Infantry in the Grade Two John Francome Novice. The Jukebox Man, who gave the former football manager the biggest win of his long ownership career in last year’s King George VI Chase at Kempton, took the same race on his chasing debut in November 2024, and while The Jukebox Man is currently on the sidelines due to injury, Taurus Bay promises to be an able deputy at the festival meetings as the season unfolds. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK
articles.description: Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology. The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hackers reportedly breach US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform
articles.description: Intrusion into Cloud One platform could jeopardize security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data Hackers are reported to have breached the US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform, a break-in that comes days after reports that a CIA database was accessed. Reuters reported on Friday that the intrusion into the USAF’s Cloud One platform could jeopardize the security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data. Continue reading...

articles.title: British Gas owner seeks urgent government talks over future of storage facility
articles.description: Centrica boss memo to 400 workers at gas plant off Yorkshire coast says utility doing all it can ‘to save your jobs’ The boss of the British Gas owner Centrica has told hundreds of staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham and would do everything he could to save jobs. Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter. Continue reading...

articles.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
articles.description: Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. Continue reading...

articles.title: King tides batter US coasts as storms threaten Thanksgiving celebrations
articles.description: Heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding creating hazardous conditions for millions travelling for holiday King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a turbulent Thanksgiving period, with severe weather threatening millions across the country. Along the California coast, king tides caused considerable damage. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, large waves battered the coastline on Wednesday, destroying part of a pier and sending debris into the ocean. The National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings covering parts of the Pacific coastline and shorelines around San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay. Several beachfront properties in Pacifica have already experienced flooding, while authorities in Marin County temporarily issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront homes at Stinson Beach. Continue reading...

articles.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
articles.description: Greenpeace publishes report showing tech firm is continuing to build despite planning appeal still unresolved Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval. “Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Punched in the guts’: Poundland staff left reeling as it goes into administration
articles.description: Workers are sad but unsurprised as closures and job losses loom, while 2,000 suppliers will take a big hit Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? “I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it. While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights
articles.description: Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances. The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical. Continue reading...

articles.title: A bakery, a playground, a speaker’s corner … how a former Brussels car garage tore up the art gallery rulebook
articles.description: Repurposing a space previously used for selling Citroëns, the Belgian capital now has its first ever dedicated space for contemporary art. It’s certainly ambitious – but will they be able to fill it? ‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night. Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. The original Parisian Pompidou was designed as a transformable cultural machine for the city ; this place takes those urban ambitions to an even greater extreme. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I’m like a lamp-post. Not glam, but vital’: Jennifer Reid, the singer saving the Industrial Revolution’s working-class songs
articles.description: She started out scribbling 19th-century workers’ songs on receipts at her retail job. Now, the folk disruptor is taking them global – and finding resonances with today’s injustices When Jennifer Reid was working in Home Bargains, she used till receipts to write out the folk ballads she was learning by heart, and then tucked them into her waistband, because staff uniforms didn’t have pockets. “Or if it was too sweaty in summer, I’d hide them behind the shampoo bottles and then go back for them,” she recalls. Growing up in Middleton, Greater Manchester, Reid discovered local broadside ballads – single-sheet songs sold on the street depicting life and events, which boomed during the Industrial Revolution – when volunteering at Chetham’s Library in her late teens. Reid describes her years prior to this as being “a cantankerous young ’un with all this energy that was sometimes misdirected into antisocial stuff” but this new direction was mind-expanding. “I’d never thought about Oldham or Rochdale in a historical cultural context before,” she says. “Very soon I realised: I want to make sure this history doesn’t die.” Continue reading...

articles.title: A Ghost Story for Christmas: The Bride’s Chamber review – Mark Gatiss just made his best spooky festive tale yet
articles.description: Fast becoming an essential Christmas tradition, the Sherlock creator’s latest in this classic horror series – starring Martin Freeman, effectively playing Charles Dickens – is inventive, joyous and, at times, genuinely terrifying For all the doom and gloom about the death of Christmas television as a collective event – nice try bunging on a normal Friday schedule with the word “Christmas” in front of each show, ITV, but we see you – can we at least agree that the most unsung festive TV tradition is Mark Gatiss’s continued revival of A Ghost Story for Christmas? For years now, it has functioned as a dark mirror to the Julia Donaldson animations. Each new episode is small and self-contained, clearly made on a shoestring but containing at least one moment of bone-deep foundational horror. And, as much as this might make the purists clutch their pearls, I would argue that the Gatiss run – starting in earnest in 2018 after a 2013 one-off, with a fallow year for Covid – deserves to be seen as the pinnacle of the series. True, the 1970s version contained classics including The Signalman and A Warning to the Curious, but only eight of those were made. The Bride’s Chamber is Gatiss’s ninth.

articles.title: Get me a 747 and deploy the oxygen masks! The British pilot behind Hollywood’s greatest inflight scenes
articles.description: An emergency landing for Bridesmaids, a humiliation for Ben Stiller in Focker-in-Law, a giant toilet for Britney Spears in the Toxic video … Richard Chan, No 1 provider of airplane cabin sets, recalls his finest work With Thanksgiving having just kicked off holiday season in the US, millions of people are boarding flights, many more concerned than ever about how chaotic that might be. Aside from the shock of the recent FAA shutdown , not a day seems to go by without a viral video of someone behaving badly or being removed from an airplane: Saturday Night Live even did a sketch about the introduction of a “new airline class” , with a whole section of a plane reserved for “crazy people”. In the big Thanksgiving movie Focker-In-Law , Ben Stiller has a lengthy and awkward encounter with a flight attendant who is summoned by a passenger called Olivia, played by Ariana Grande. On arrival, he learns that Olivia is his potential daughter-in-law and, of course, that means more trouble with his ex-CIA father-in-law Jack, played by Robert De Niro. Continue reading...

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be
articles.description: Working out where returning hero Steve Rogers has been is only one of the multiversal puzzles fans must now get their heads around – which is catnip for the connoisseurs The cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday is now roughly three weeks away and, judging by the final trailer , we’re living in the one timeline where every loose end Marvel has left dangling for years is now worth tugging on. Even the ones we thought the studio had tied up rather nicely. Ever since it became apparent that Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers would be returning in the new film, along with next year’s sequel Avengers: Secret Wars, fans have been asking themselves: where exactly has he been all this time? Now, thanks to the latest footage, we’re beginning to get an idea, and we might also be starting to pick up clues as to why Doctor Doom would take an interest in his new postcode. One of the most startling aspects of the new trailer is the arrival of the Fantastic Four, led by Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards, on Rogers’ front lawn. We’ve known since the finale of Avengers: Endgame that Steve used Tony Stark’s newly discovered time-travelling tech to go back to the 1940s and live out his life with Peggy Carter during

articles.title: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
articles.description: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’” In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually r

articles.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the pyrotechnic emotions of club-pop kid Tsatsamis
articles.description: Fusing George Michael’s vocal and stage presence with Sophie’s tactile beats, the singer packs his floor-filling anthems with dramatic catharsis From Buckinghamshire, UK Recommended if you like George Michael, Patrick Cowley, Sophie Up next Supporting Jessie Ware on tour in the UK and Ireland until 5 December Ask an actor and they’ll tell you the best way to perform a character who’s drunk or high is often the subtlest. Anyone can play a mess; it’s more interesting to watch someone cling to their slipping sense of poise. Many of Peter Tsatsamis-Cooper’s songs occupy a hard-partying mindset, but all of them find the singer caught up in big emotions, as his composure slowly, then suddenly, gives way to pyrotechnic displays of feeling. Continue reading...

articles.title: The month’s best folk album: Lizabett Russo confronts her roots on an odyssey through Transylvania
articles.description: (Last Night from Glasgow) Russo’s latest album Pe Unde Trece Dorul, roughly translated as Where Longing Goes, is full of surprises – and shows what a fantastically versatile singer she is Long based in Scotland, Lizabett Russo returns to her native Romania for her fifth album of idiosyncratic, spectral folk. Having defied her parents’ wishes to leave the country age 18 and commence her musical journey, she travelled through Transylvania’s remote villages to learn doine (songs) and strigături (traditional rhymed shouts/calls), and named her album after a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, a woman awarded a title to aim for by the Romanian National Institute of Heritage: Living Human Treasure. “Dorul” is like the Welsh hiraeth or Galician saudade , referencing longing and homesickness, and “trece” explains how these feelings travel, wander and pass. Released by the label that also put out Dick Gaughan ’s startling R/Evolution box set, Russo’s album begins like an update of Fourth World music created by trumpeter Jon Hassell and Brian Eno. A sly two-note guitar riff, Tim Lane’s soft drums, and Călin Han’s slowly blown kaval flutter coolness into the air, then Russo joins, multi

articles.title: Pummelling electronic trio Factory Floor’s first album in a decade shows signs of mellowing – but is it all a feint?
articles.description: (Phantasy Sound) One of the buzziest acts of the 2010s return with One Trip, which bathes their classic sound in a warmer light – until the buzzsaw synths and scattershot percussion explode Devotees still speak in hushed awe about the intense, hypnotic performances by Factory Floor, one of the buzziest electronic groups of the 2010s. Even the band agree: Nik Colk Void (vocalist and modular synth wrangler) wistfully remembered them as “full of carnage” during their lengthy hiatus. So what on earth went down at Mutek Montreal in 2024? Their one-off reunion show proved so transformative that it inspired Factory Floor’s first album in 10 years. Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serr

articles.title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels
articles.description: A countdown to Christmas; musical mice; archeological treasure; a disgraced magician; a terrifying curse and more And a Partridge in a Pear Tree by Fay Evans, illustrated by Jono Ganz, Flying Eye, £8.99 Partridge’s solitary splendour is rudely and cumulatively interrupted in this riotous, collage picture-book version of the well-loved carol – with a humorous twist at the end. Lost and Found at the Gurdwara by Baljinder Kaur, Farshore, £7.99 Darshan is getting ready for the Nagar Kirtan procession with her grandparents, Bibi and Baba – but things keep going missing. This resplendent search-and-find picture book is a gorgeously detailed and evocative guide to traditional Sikh celebrations. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Private Diary of Pope Francis review – a glimpse of life inside the Vatican
articles.description: The former pontiff’s edited journals show piety and humility, but his deeper motivations remain a mystery When the cardinals in Rome elected the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio as the 266th pope of the Roman Catholic church in March 2013 – the first Latin American, the first pontiff born outside Europe since the 8th century, the first Jesuit and the first to take the name Francis (after Saint Francis of Assisi) – many of us lapsed Catholics gave a small cheer. Here was a man who looked fair to change the increasingly fusty and conservative, authoritarian and admonitory, tendencies of his two predecessors. Bergoglio seemingly did not want the ceremonial trappings of the office – he’d bought himself a return ticket home to Buenos Aires and caught the bus back to the Vatican guest house where the other cardinals were staying, insisting he would not be moving into the papal apartments overlooking St Peter’s Square. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s the biggest ever month for video games – so why am I playing a title from 2006? | Dominik Diamond
articles.description: While everyone else is giddy over Zelda and GTA, Dominik Diamond finds himself behind the times on a Nintendo Wii I find myself on the wrong side of gaming history this month. I have zero zeitgeist. My takes are as fresh as something found at the rear of the fridge. I haven’t even played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but we’ll get to that. Worse, all month, the Nintendo sector of the gaming world has been going googly eyed over Zelda. The Ocarina of Time remake seems to have produced more joy than all the puppies in the world. But not for me. I have never liked Zelda. It’s like being a movie reviewer who doesn’t like Disney, or a vegan shark. Continue reading...

articles.title: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities
articles.description: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

articles.title: DJ Tink, drop the beat! Peter Pan hits Club NVRLND for some noughties nostalgia
articles.description: The Vaults, London X Factor’s Diana Vickers leads this trip back to the 00s, as JM Barrie’s story is retooled as a night of pop bangers How about if Peter Pan, refusing to grow up, was a stunted man-boy lost in the what-ifs of his youth? He might be the promoter of a noughties club night, stuck in his glory days where everyone’s dressed like Girls Aloud meets the Vengaboys and the world hasn’t yet gone into meltdown. NVRLAND is that club, and this show – created by Steven Kunis and Jack Holden – is halfway between a jukebox musical and a cheesy disco, masterminded, surely, for the Christmas party crowd to down oversweet cocktails before oversharing with someone they barely know from the finance department. It’s basically pantomime for millennials/zillennials, with lots of audience participation from the dancefloor. And after a bit of warming up, it is great, giddy fun. Continue reading...

articles.title: Teeny tiny Tracey Emin, the mother of the Moomins and Latvia’s Nazi murders – the week in art
articles.description: Small-scale paintings by the Margate avant garde, a celebration of Tove Jannson, and a homage to psychiatric patients killed by the Third Reich – all in your weekly dispatch Tove Jansson and Her Families Christmas fun starts early with this celebration of the Finnish artist and illustrator who created the Moomins. • Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration, London, until 9 May Continue reading...

articles.title: Play about 12-year-old ecojustice influencer wins Shakespeare’s Globe prize
articles.description: Timothy X Atack wrote Tiny Alarms after workshops with children, who felt theirs would be the last generation of humans Tiny, a 12-year-old schoolgirl, is an ecojustice influencer, whose funny and disconcerting takes on the climate crisis go viral. She is also an alien, sent to warn humankind of its impending doom – but her mission is far more difficult than she anticipated. This is the plot of Tiny Alarms, the first winner of Shakespeare’s Globe’s new climate playwriting prize. It was inspired by the real beliefs of schoolchildren for whom its author, Timothy X Atack, ran creative writing workshops exploring ideas around the far future. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lessons in Love and Violence – royal power play delivers huge impact with minimal means
articles.description: Queen Elizabeth Hall, London George Benjamin and Martin Crimp’s opera was given a skeletal staging where every detail spoke volumes, leaving the LPO to shine in the spotlight It is always a shock to realise how little apparatus theatre really needs. Dan Ayling’s semi-staging of George Benjamin and Martin Crimp ’s 2018 opera played out across a shallow strip in front of the London Philharmonic Orchestra, with singers occasionally slipping between conductor Edward Gardner and the front desks of the strings. Props were minimal but significant: a skipping rope, a glass tumbler, a pot containing a child’s ashes, a crown spotlit on a velvet cushion. There was no set, just five chairs on one side of the podium and one on the other: a succinct image of isolation, of power dynamics skewed. The protagonists of this grim drama about Edward II – the King, his lover, Gaveston, his wife, Isabel, her ally Mortimer – wore sleek black tie except utilitarian, ambitious, underdressed Mortimer. As the Boy was manoeuvred into position as Young King, tenor James Way not only stood taller and held himself more pugnaciously but also put on a tie: every detail spoke volumes. Continue reading...

The 46-year-old is a fiendish perfectionist and a fierce champion of every last ingredient. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop. Elite cooking while talking like a Bren gun is a skill she’s honed, first in cookery demos “talking to a plastic bag and a stray dog, and you’d be lucky if someone came over to shelter from the rain”; then on Saturday Kitchen – a trial by fire: “Everything is easy after that. articles.title: Figs trees grow well in the UK – here’s everything you need to know to plant one
articles.description: These exotics can bear plenty of fruit, but you will need a firm hand to stop them dominating your patch You might imagine figs would be tricky to grow in cooler climates like the UK’s (heatwaves aside). But you’d be wrong! Figs can do remarkably well – some might say too well – in this segment of the northern hemisphere. In favourable conditions, fig trees can be quite the thug, inclined to take up any and all the space available for their roving roots. One enormous specimen behind a train station near where I grew up has been there for decades, occupying an impressive number of square metres. You can, of course, purchase a fig tree from a plant nursery. But the two I have in my garden were both grown from hardwood cuttings taken when the parent plant was dormant, which makes now a good time to give this slow but generally reliable process a try. Alternatively, you can wait until spring and seek out a parent plant that’s producing suckers to pot up. Continue reading...

They have lost seven matches in a row against Ireland: there was a time when such a statistic would have been unimaginable. Sam Prendergast kicked brilliantly, off the tee and from hand, to orchestrate a success that was a classic Irish blend of power and finesse. This may be an opportune moment to snap up pre-Christmas bargains on the high street but Maro Itoje and his side are rather more intent on securing a priceless little chunk of history. Never before in 121 years have England’s men beaten New Zealand in three consecutive Tests and the last time their opponents lost six times in a calendar year was back in 1949. During that distant annus horribilis the All Blacks ended up contesting simultaneous Test series against South Africa and Australia and lost them both; this time around there would be no such asterisk. articles.title: The explosion of extreme wealth is the major problem of our time | Bernie Sanders

Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class. Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.” Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Why Knot?
articles.description: Why Knot? By Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist of Rabobank De Cos they said so. European leaders have selected the former head of the Spanish central bank to replace ECB president Lagarde over his Dutch peer. De Cos’ nomination is a deal in which German economist Brunnermeier and French economist Laurence Boone will both get a seat at the table as well. Staff changes will happen over a matter of months starting in January, when Schnabel makes place for Boone.  The Spanish candidate is generally seen as leaning less hawkish than Klaas Knot, but arguably the German pick for Brunnermeier is the more interesting one. Brunnermeier is not the traditional Bundesbank hawk. In fact, he was one of the proponents of a plan to create Eurozone-wide safe assets, the so-called ESBies .  Contrast that to current German member of the Executive Board. Isabel Schnabel has been one of the more hawkish policymakers at the central bank. So, Brunnermeier could mark a change in tone. But the German has also expressed caution about inflation signals and the impact of QE. So, it may take a crisis –or at least some very difficult policy choices– to reveal the latent preferences of the new leadership.

articles.description: Europe Being 'Flooded With Cocaine' By Cartel Speedboat Swarms As Police Admit They're Outgunned Drug traffickers are running cocaine into Europe aboard fleets of high-powered speedboats off southern Spain, and Spain's own government counted more than 600 of the so-called go-fast boats in the Strait of Gibraltar last year , calling them a "major threat" in its annual security report . A Spanish security source said authorities have been left underequipped to deal with the narcolanchas. Guardia Civil officers pursue a ‘narcolanchas’ drug smuggling boat ( Guardia Civil/The Independent ) The boats, known in Spain as narcolanchas, carry up to four outboard engines totaling some 1,200 horsepower and can top 80 knots (92mph), well beyond what most patrol boats can match. Crews typically leave northern Morocco at night loaded with South American cocaine, meet larger supply boats offshore for fuel, food and fresh crew, then race for remote beaches, river mouths and estuaries in Andalusia, where lookouts and vehicles wait to move the drugs inland. articles.title: Thousands of girls and women report bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas
articles.description: Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily. French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order). Continue reading...

articles.title: Labour’s EU reset deal will be ‘floor not ceiling’, says Burnham cabinet ally
articles.description: Scottish secretary Douglas Alexander to say Britain cannot secure the change it needs ‘without changing our relationship with Europe’ Labour’s EU reset deal will be a “floor not a ceiling”, according to a close cabinet ally of Andy Burnham, who says the UK has been a “cork bobbing on the tides of history” because of the power lost by Brexit. Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, will tell a conference in Italy on Friday that the government cannot deliver the major change Britain needs “without changing our relationship with Europe. When the status quo is not working, you don’t stand still. You move forward. When the status quo is broken, you don’t ignore it. You fix it.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
articles.description: Body urged Bristol city council to reject plan because of risk to nearby protected wildlife and habitats Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser. The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site. articles.title: Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power | Eoghan Gilmartin
articles.description: Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP). articles.title: UK’s taste for cow’s milk sours as sales hit record low
articles.description: Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began. Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?
articles.description: Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe? Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what. She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Sunrise on the Reaping: The new Hunger Games film is a gen Z call to action – critics have missed the point | Rafqa Touma
articles.description: We’ve been brought up on literature about underdogs who fight – and triumph – against an unjust status quo I first read The Hunger Games trilogy in early high school. Set in the post-apocalyptic nation of Panem, society is ruled by the Capitol – they are fascistic, surveil everything, and keep the middle and upper classes quiet with annual reality war games in which lower-class teenagers must fight to the death. Ten years later, in 2020, I was about to enter a newsroom for the first time, at the tail end of Donald Trump’s first presidency. That same year, Suzanne Collins returned to her dystopian world with a prequel. The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes is set decades before the original trilogy, revealing the origin story of both the games and their architect, President Snow, through his young, possessive perspective. Continue reading...
