articles.title: Finals weekend will show who really holds rugby power heading into World Cup year | Ugo Monye
articles.description: England can maintain their trajectory against a tired New Zealand, but how France handle South Africa in the final will offer significant insight We are approaching the end of what has been a wild year for England. It has been 12 months of either feast or famine, of boom or bust. The worst ever Six Nations performance followed by another fine autumn as they head into Saturday’s rematch with the All Blacks. Their lowest ebb under Steve Borthwick in Rome and their best performance last weekend since he took charge. Without getting ahead of ourselves, the next Six Nations has taken on a very different complexion after this month’s results and performances. There is a big, humble reminder given that England enjoyed a clean sweep last autumn and then endured such a disappointing Six Nations, but there is a different feel about them 12 months on. Despite the winning run that England were on, there was still grumbling about their playing style. That is no longer the case. They have performed well at their home stadium in front of sold-out crowds and with millions of people being able to watch them on TV each week. Continue reading...

articles.title: Manchester United extend Fernandes contract until 2028 to stop free transfer
articles.description: Club activate option and plan further talks with captain ‘I am not nice,’ says Pochettino as he targets improvement Manchester United have triggered a clause to extend the captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract until the summer of 2028 on a day when Mauricio Pochettino warned his players they should not expect him to be “nice” in his attempts to turn around the club’s fortunes. Fernandes’ deal was due to expire in June and by exercising the option United have avoided the risk from January that he could negotiate a pre-contract agreement with a club abroad to join on a free next summer. Fernandes said this month that talks over a longer extension were on hold “because of the context of the team and the club”. He has turned down two United contract offers. Continue reading...

articles.title: Overton’s fiery five-wicket haul helps England to flip Gabba script against Australia
articles.description: No ground in Australia is more associated with ritual guttings of English cricket teams than the so-called Gabbatoir. They usually leave in a state of disarray, beaten up on the field and with ears still ringing from abuse on the boundary’s edge. Yet on a muggy Friday night on Vulture Street, the locals had precious little material to work with and the traditional script was flipped on its head. Driven by Jamie Overton’s fiery five-wicket haul, England wiped the floor with their hosts for the second match in a row to claim a 2-1 lead with two to play. Continue reading...

articles.title: Football Daily | Watford, the Pozzos and the hottest managerial seat in the game
articles.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic, Xisco Muñoz, Claudio Ranieri, Roy Hodgson, Rob Edwards, Slaven Bilic, Chris Wilder, Valérien Ismael, Tom Cleverley, Paulo Pezzolano and Edward Still in being sacked by the Pozzo family since 2012. There was no denial on Sunday, when the axe inevitably fell on the head coach following a 4-0 shellacking at Sheffield United and the Italian left after only 18 games in charge. While his reign is unlikely to live long in the memory of anyone at Vicarage Road, Dionisi can at least boast on his LinkedIn page that in terms of longevity under the Pozzos, he took charge of 18 more matches than Dyche, 17 more than García and 16 more than McKinlay. Indeed, he even outlasted Rob Edwards, who was assured he would be backed “come hell or high water” upon his 2022 appointment, only to be fired from the ejector seat 11 games later. Continue reading...

articles.title: A third of rough sleepers offered bed or support after Burnham Christmas vow
articles.description: Campaigners accuse ministers of hiding how many offers were turned down as PM hails ‘early progress’ UK politics live – latest updates Just over a third of rough sleepers have been offered a bed or support as a result of Andy Burnham’s pledge to get people off the streets by Christmas, but campaigners have accused ministers of hiding how many offers were turned down. Data published on Friday showed at least 3,276 people sleeping rough were offered a route off the street in October, under the new scheme announced by the prime minister on his first day in office . That compares with an estimated 9,369 who slept rough across England in September, the latest month where data was available. Continue reading...

articles.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
articles.description: Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights. In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning , the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights. articles.description: Americans Set To Put A Record $21 Billion Of Christmas On Buy-Now-Pay-Later... Mostly From Their Phones Adobe expects American shoppers to put a record $21.3 billion of their online holiday spending on buy now, pay later loans this season, up 6.6% from last year , according to its forecast for Nov. 1 through Dec. 31. On Cyber Monday alone, shoppers are expected to finance $1.09 billion online , the second year in a row BNPL tops $1 billion on Cyber Monday. Black Friday adds another $807 million. And 82% of BNPL spending will come through phones rather than desktops , which Adobe chalks up to "impulse shopping." BNPL drove $20 billion of online holiday spending last season, up nearly 10%, as we reported in January, and Cyber Monday 2025 was the biggest BNPL day on record, at over $1 billion . The loans ride on a bigger number: Adobe sees Americans spending $275.1 billion online this holiday season, up 6.7% , with Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, bringing in $47.5 billion (up 7.4%), or 17.3% of the season. articles.title: Venezuela Admits Its $237.5 Billion Debt Is Unsustainable
articles.description: Venezuela Admits Its $237.5 Billion Debt Is Unsustainable Authored by Evgenia Filimianova via The Epoch Times , Venezuela has set out a plan to restructure $237.5 billion in debt, restore stability, and more than double its oil output. Caracas said in a macroeconomic framework published on Tuesday that the country's total debt, about 242 percent of GDP, is unsustainable and that Venezuela has been in protracted default since 2017. Venezuela's economy has been battered by years of hyperinflation, sanctions and, most recently, deadly earthquakes. Venezuela, currently led by interim leader Delcy Rodríguez since the U.S. military captured former leader Nicolás Maduro in January, said it would pursue a single, comprehensive restructuring of debt owed by both the state and state oil company PDVSA, but did not specify how much relief it is seeking . The largest block is about $110 billion in Eurobonds, around $46 billion of it unpaid interest. The rest comprises arbitration claims, bilateral and multilateral loans, bank debt, and PDVSA's supplier, pension, and other nonfinancial liabilities, some of which are owed within the public sector. articles.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
articles.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.title: Houseplant hacks: does grouping plants together increase humidity?
articles.description: It will help during winter months, but there are better solutions for really thirsty plants The problem With the onset of winter, the heating comes on, humidity drops and tropical plants that yearn for rainforest conditions end up in something closer to a desert. Cue crispy leaf edges. Humidifiers work, but they require buying, filling and cleaning. Misting works, but you need to remember to do it. So, a free, lazy alternative has an obvious appeal. The hack This hack is based on transpiration. Plants constantly release water vapour through their leaves, so huddling them together raises the humidity around them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: A close watch on this autumn’s leaf fall – it’s been unpredictable | Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
articles.description: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line. Continue reading...

articles.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
articles.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. articles.description: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. articles.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
articles.description: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy Continue reading...

articles.description: Even the best managers can struggle to escape ex-players’ need to manufacture a crisis for content. Enter Michael Carrick … A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick. Neville: Just so you know, we’re already filming. This is the intro bit, where we show everyone coming on to set and doing some light banter. It humanises us. The viewer sees it and thinks we’re just mates chatting about football, rather than scions of a global podcast empire commercially obliged to produce an endless scroll of provocative content for money. articles.description: Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found. articles.title: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’
articles.description: As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear You ’ ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJax No. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus. What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and imp

articles.title: You’re cracking me up: cinema’s greatest egg scenes – ranked!
articles.description: As You Can See Everything’s contention whisking scene beats movie-goers into a frenzy, here’s a taster of the most eggstraordinary moments on film It’s breakfast time at the California home of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced former CEO of blood-testing company Theranos, and as the camera follows her lightly forking some eggs, boyfriend Billy Evans swoops in, grabs the bowl off her and begins demonstrating how it should be done. articles.title: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago
articles.description: Bournemouth International Centre Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer. Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC we

articles.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes
articles.description: Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills , just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK . The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains. Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire Continue reading...

articles.title: Children’s hospitals close beds to comply with NHS cost-cutting targets
articles.description: Sheffield children’s hospital, Liverpool’s Alder Hey and London’s Great Ormond Street make cuts amid efforts to major savings Children’s hospitals are closing beds and shedding staff to comply with swingeing cost-cutting targets set by NHS chiefs to stop the health service overspending. articles.title: Marlboro maker Altria considering takeover bid for Imperial Brands

Altria, whose Philip Morris division makes Marlboro and Benson & Hedges cigarettes, told the City on Thursday that it was considering an offer. If made it was likely to be solely in cash, it said. articles.description: The sector is in retreat across parts of the county, with developments paused. articles.title: Ministry of Defence signs £8.7bn deal with Babcock to maintain submarines

articles.title: Novelist’s first album in eight years has Skepta, skits and soul – and showcases a true British original
articles.description: ( Mashwrks) Sharp, unsentimental rhymes and a fearless disregard for genre make Scenes a richly varied victory lap for for one of grime’s most distinctive talents It’s not often that a UK rap album arrives accompanied by its own air freshener and video game, but here we are. Head over to Novelist’s website, and you can find not merely the usual means of promoting a new release – branded hoodies, T-shirts and so on – but a scented mirror hanger that bears the album’s artwork and Scenes: the Drive, a vaguely Mario Kart-ish arcade game that involves driving around the landmarks of London and Los Angeles avoiding buses and the attentions of the traffic police to the strains of an album track called Prime. But then, from the moment he appeared on the grime scene in his teens – so young he now constitutes an elder statesman in his late 20s – the south Londoner has cut something of a maverick figure in the world of UK rap. He arrived bearing a moniker that seemed oddly bookish among his more grittily named peers. His early releases saw him working alongside defiantly left-field producer Mumdance. He attracted a lot of press attention of the “grime’s brightest new hope” variety, but seemed

articles.title: Tonight the Music Seems So Loud by Sathnam Sanghera audiobook review – in praise of George Michael
articles.description: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singer When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess. This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders). Continue reading...

articles.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power
articles.description: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bring me the scrotum stapler! Is this the world’s most extreme performance artist?
articles.description: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best reds and whites from the golden state: our pick of Californian wines
articles.description: Having built its reputation on big, brash reds, the centre of US winemaking is keeping pace with changing tastes and now becoming known for crisp whites, too I was always more of a Dawson’s Creek girlie than a fan of The OC , yet the subject of this column has found me wrestling with the earworm that is the latter’s theme tune : “California, here we come/Right back where we started from.” For Scribe Winery , at the southern end of the Sonoma Valley, this is apt, though I’m not sure winemaker Andrew Mariani would thank me for the comparison. Since buying 100 hectares here in 2007, he and his brother, Adam, have been restoring the land to viticulture after an interlude as a turkey farm. Some of the Marianis’ vines are riesling and sylvaner, honouring the German immigrant family who first cultivated them here in the 1850s, but they make up a small proportion of Scribe’s production, which is focused on bright, bracing chardonnay and terroir-driven pinot noir. It’s an approach that reflects the trend of drinkers turning away from the beefy reds, particularly cabernet sauvignon, that made California famous, towards fresher – dare I say Old World? – styles. Andrew has pulled up “cab” on r

articles.title: Citrus bars, mandarin drizzle cake, boozy compote and a lime bundt: Natalie Paull’s citrus bakes – recipes
articles.description: These mouthwatering sweet treats are a sure tang My favourite cool-weather cocktail plus caramel meet the acidic burst of citrus segments. You can make this with any orange citrus, but I feel small mandarins must be included. I take the extra meditative time to scratch the white, fibrous fuzz of pith away and slice horizontally to make a cute flower shapes. Sometimes I’ll add a few skin-intact cumquats with their sour, tangy insides. If blood oranges are around, I’ll include them with anything from a demure vein of maroon to the Carrie -esque carmine of late-season fruit. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for bread buns with cheese and apple | A kitchen in Rome
articles.description: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet. Continue reading...

articles.title: Thursday news quiz: Plagiarism claims, eye-strain games and a stranded little bear
articles.description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare? The Thursday quiz always loves an animal story with a happy ending. Having survived a premature birth in 2017 – she arrived so early she couldn’t stand on her own – she had become a global sensation. articles.title: Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’
articles.description: Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts “I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.” It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . articles.title: Do you want to waste 15 minutes of your life reading the Reformer by Nigel Farage? | John Crace
articles.description: Or maybe just throw it in the recycling – every future issue could be written in German anyway if Burnham gets his way It’s the “choice of a lifetime”. articles.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
articles.description: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. articles.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1 When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.” They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. articles.title: Some old-school advice for Burnham: boost competition if you want growth | Nils Pratley
articles.description: Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’ The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government. articles.title: The Guardian view on Russia’s war dead: the toll won’t stop Putin. Resolve in backing Ukraine remains essential | Editorial
articles.description: New data offers shocking details of military fatalities. But without domestic accountability, only external pressure can end this conflict The toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine is appallingly evident in the devastation of apartment blocks and hospitals, in the suffering of survivors and, above all, in the mourning of the dead, which included an estimated 150,000 soldiers and at least 18,000 civilians. The toll on Russia’s population has been carefully obscured by Moscow. But a fuller picture has emerged from its own statistics after the hacking group Cyber Partisans, linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow obtained 11m death certificates. Analysis by the Guardian offers disturbing insights into the deaths of almost half a million Russians in Ukraine since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on fostering: ceremonies and sibling rights should help care leavers | Editorial
articles.description: Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeper The first lifelong guardianship ceremonies , held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life. Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds. Care leavers are over-represented in prisons and homeless shelters, and among those who are not in education, employment or training. In August, the Department for Education published an analysis of 112 deaths

articles.title: Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS | Letter
articles.description: Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS ( Letters, 18 November ). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades. Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected. Continue reading...

articles.description: Widening pathways for disadvantaged youngsters from Europe should be top of the agenda in discussions about fees, says Angela McRobbie It is dispiriting to hear arguments against young people from the EU being able to attend British universities with fees reset to home student level ( EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates, 25 November ). articles.title: Ofsted’s pedagogically pinheaded approach to inspections | Letters

articles.title: Thomas Frank earns first Crystal Palace win as McNeil cuts down Real Sociedad
articles.description: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

They have been asked by Democrats on the House judiciary committee to give evidence as efforts gather pace to examine Gianni Infantino’s failed FFE scheme along with links between Fifa and the Trump administration. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump alleges ‘fake’ economic figures released before US midterms but doesn’t provide evidence

articles.description: Brighton Dome Boasting all their surviving members, the quartet put on an extraordinarily eclectic and entertaining show, held together by pure ferocity Few punk bands looked destined to make old bones – longevity wasn’t really the point – but you might have got particularly long odds on the Damned lasting any kind of distance. They were “the Bash Street Kids of punk”, in writer Jon Savage’s memorable estimation: “While other groups were carefully considering their moves,” he wrote, “the Damned went out there and pulled faces at the world as if there was no tomorrow.” Even their debut single New Rose implied they knew their time was limited: “I better go,” sang Dave Vanian amid its frantic thunder, “or it’ll be too late.” How wrong can you be? Their peers are long gone or too riven by bad blood to work together, but the Damned are the one major punk band to observe the movement’s 50th anniversary with every surviving original member onstage, something you get the impression even the Damned are faintly startled by. “This is the kind of venue that would have told us to fuck off 50 years ago,” muses guitarist Captain Sensible, as he gazes around the Dome’s stately auditorium. Impressi

articles.title: Mammy Goose is well and truly cooked in Glasgow’s incredibly random Aladdin
articles.description: King’s theatre, Glasgow The offensive stereotypes have been ditched but this glitzy panto starring Elaine C Smith shoehorns in plenty of irrelevant material Staging a traditional Aladdin in 2026 is problematic. All those laundry scenes, acrobatics and faux Chinese names have the unpleasant whiff of orientalism. In that sense, it is good to see this glitzy mainstream panto, scripted by Alan McHugh for Crossroads, ditching all that. If only it had not thrown the genie out with the bath water. Stereotypes aside, Aladdin can still be a gripping coming-of-age story about greed and gullibility, poverty and power. The stakes can be loaded with deceit, jeopardy and cunning. In this version, set in the land of Pantomania, almost none of that survives. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Utterly compelling’: Black Gold, a raging oil field fire set to music, is like a scream from nature
articles.description: Manchester Collective, Lakeside Arts, Nottingham This take on Luke Mombrea’s Novello-winning work about a fire that burned for two months in Santa Fe, had little need of its billowing video backdrop Premieres are all well and good, but what about second performances, and third and fourth? We puzzle over the problem of new music, of how to build a living classical repertoire, while too often giving new works just one outing to make their case, audiences just one chance to hear them. How brilliant, then, to see American composer Luke Mombrea’s Black Gold – winner of a 2025 Ivor Novello award – at the centre of the Manchester Collective’s new tour: another chance to get our ears around this widescreen soundscape with its slippery electro-acoustic vistas. The fire that raged through the Santa Fe oil fields in 1928 burned for two months, swallowing up the surrounding desert in smoke and ash. Steel plate photographs show derricks dwarfed by pillars of flame and black billowing clouds. articles.title: ‘Everybody tells me how I can keep working. My answer begins with ‘F’ and ends with ‘off’: Mike Leigh on 55 years of films – and why he’s just made his last
articles.description: The acclaimed director has announced his latest film Tender Loving Care will be his last. He talks about coming to terms with a life-changing condition and how he would have loved to have made a big budget modern-day movie Mike Leigh and his partner, the actor Marion Bailey, were knocking around at home last Christmas, looking for a good film to watch and constantly coming up short. Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. It’s just that Topsy-Turvy happens to be a very enjoyable watch.” The way Leigh sees it, his films are like children. They’ve outgrown him, moved on, but it’s nice to check the family ties are still strong. Some are sunny (Life is Sweet; Happy-Go-Lucky) and some are dour (Naked; Hard Truths), but they all share the same DNA, the same real-world interests and tragicomic mindset. He can’t choose between them; he’ll defend each one to the death. Then he pauses and says, “But I’ve got a soft spot for Meantime.” Continue reading

articles.description: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’v

articles.title: Liam Delap’s struggles are symbolic of damaging Chelsea churn
articles.description: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer. On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place. Continue reading...

The forwards coach, Jason Ryan, has said that “there is not much juice in the tank” while Graham Henry, who led them to the 2011 World Cup title, has continued the theme in even starker terms. “It’s the end of the season and we’re buggered. They’ve just got no gas in the tank.” It is understood that narrative has raised a number of eyebrows within the England camp. The view, as England seek to clinch a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time in the history of the fixture, is best summed up as, “welcome to our world”. We are nearing the end of a gruelling year for the All Blacks, who give the impression they cannot wait for their season to end, but the grind in England, that which led to Maro Itoje being ordered to take the summer off, is at the very least comparable. Continue reading...

articles.title: Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List review – the comfort show of my happiest dreams
articles.description: The comedian knows how to make perfectly relaxing TV – even as he tries heart-racing new experiences with celebrity pals. From flying a plane loop-the-loop with Mel Giedroyc to bungee jumping with Joanne McNally, it is bliss Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List, in which burgeoning national treasure since last year’s win on The Celebrity Traitors Alan tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, is filler TV of the most obvious kind. But this particular varietal has a twist. In this show in which the presenter tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, the presenter feels under no pressure to complete any of the tasks he doesn’t fancy. This makes the Great Big Bucket List the programme of my dreams and Alan my soulmate, my spirit animal, my safe space. Who wants to see people suffering? Pushed beyond their comfort zones? Not me. Why is the world so obsessed with making people uncomfortable? Comfort is the aim . Comfort is great . Comfort is everything . Continue reading...
